To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Candida albicans is the predominant yeast in oral candidosis in HIV‐inflicted patients.

the shift of causative organisms in HIV‐infec‐tions is not only a phenomenon in the esophagus but also in the oral cavity, and that the shift of organisms may be a consequence of the antifungal treatment.
the shift of causative organisms in oral and esophageal Candidosis under treatment with azole antifungals is a common phenomenon in immunosuppressed patients.
In summary, our research is concerned with

a) the detection of C. albicans and C. glabrata in oral and esophageal samples of HIV‐infected individuals, b) the evaluation of the efficacy of oral azole treatment in HIV‐infec‐ted patients with oral candidosis, c) the determination of the susceptibility of C. albican and C. glab‐rata to azole drugs and d) the determination of C. albica and C. glabra strains isolated before and after treatment.
the following questions: - What is the incidence of oral candidosis before and after treatment?
the question whether the change of causative organisms under antifungal treatment may influence the clinical course.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Candida albicans is the most frequently observed species in HIV‐infec‐tions.
Candida glabrta may be a causative organism in oral and esophageal Candidosis.
Candida albicans is not the only yeast that can cause oral candidosis and that other species should not be neglected in the treatment.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the use of azoles for the treatment of oral and esophageal infections in immunosuppressed patients with HIV‐infections may be followed by a change of causative organisms from C. albicans to less susceptible species.
Candida glabrateresults in more severe oral lesions than C. albican.
Candida glabrateresults in oral lesions more frequently than before and that Candida albicans is less often found after treatment.
The main takeaway from our work is that
Candida spp. are not only found as a commensal in the oral cavity of immunosuppressed patients, but can cause clinical symptoms as well.
C. glabrata is a frequent cause of oral candidosis in advanced HIV‐infected pa‐tients.
the use of fluconazole as a first line treatment in advanced stages of AIDS is not always the best option.
